## PR review: `tomorrowMs` helper in `src/date.ts`

**Verdict: request changes.** Not a hard block — the bug is real but localized and the fix is mechanical.

### The finding

`crime_00011` — **DST-Naive Day Math** (severity: medium, confidence: 0.8, agent_risk: 0.52)

Evidence verbatim:
- `+ 86400000 (day) @L52`
- `lines: 52`
- `use a calendar-aware library (Luxon, Temporal, date-fns-tz) for day math`

Summary verbatim: *"1 day-level millisecond constant in arithmetic. A day isn't 86,400,000 ms on DST-transition days; manual ms math drifts silently."*

### Why request changes (not block)

Adding 86,400,000 ms assumes every day is exactly 24 hours. In any timezone that observes DST, two days a year are **23 hours** (spring forward) or **25 hours** (fall back). On those days, `tomorrowMs(today)` lands at 11pm or 1am of the next civil day instead of the same wall-clock time tomorrow — which matters for anything user-facing (renewal reminders, "due tomorrow" UI, scheduled jobs keyed to local time).

It's "request changes" rather than block because:
- Severity is medium, not high.
- The fix is small and mechanical (swap to `Temporal.PlainDate.add({ days: 1 })`, Luxon's `plus({ days: 1 })`, or date-fns-tz's `addDays`).
- If the timestamp is only ever used as a UTC instant (e.g., a `setTimeout` of ~24h), the bug is invisible; the reviewer should ask the author which.

### The two wrong-answer days per year (US example, America/Los_Angeles 2026)

- **Sunday, March 8, 2026** — spring forward. `today` at midnight local + 86.4M ms lands at **11pm** on March 8, not midnight March 9.
- **Sunday, November 1, 2026** — fall back. `today` at midnight local + 86.4M ms lands at **1am on November 2**, not midnight November 2.

Exact dates shift by jurisdiction (EU transitions on the last Sundays of March/October; many countries observe no DST at all), but the shape is the same: one 23-hour day and one 25-hour day per year wherever DST applies.

### Side note worth flagging on the PR

`src/date.ts` already carries four other date findings (`crime_00002` Temporal Recklessness, `crime_00003` Half-UTC/Half-Local, `crime_00009` Timezone Roulette, `crime_00024` Date String Sewing, `crime_00025` Host-Locale Drift). If the team is touching this file, a single follow-up to introduce Temporal or Luxon would retire most of them together rather than playing whack-a-mole.
